newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: DOWNER DEFENDS DECISION TO ATTEND HONG KONG CEREMONY
The Foreign Affairs Minister says the swearing-in of Hong Kong's new China-appointed legislature will not mean death to democracy.
Defending his decision to attend the swearing-in ceremony, Alexander Downer reiterated the Prime Minister's stand that not attending would be against the national interest.
Mr Downer says China is determined to proceed with democratic elections in Hong Kong and the new legislature is just an interim arrangement.
He says the interests of Hong Kong and Australia are not served by covering the hand-over ceremonies in controversary.
DOWNER DESCRIBES HANSON AS A RENEGADE
Australia's Foreign Affairs Minister says most people in the Asia-Pacific region have put the racists views of Independent MP Pauline Hanson into perspective.
Alexander Downer has described Pauline Hanson as a renegade, and says she should be treated as such.
Mr Downer has downplayed her effects on trade relations within the region.
He says foreign governments are aware that the Australian Government and the vast majority of Australians completely repudiate the views that are being expressed by Pauline Hanson.
Mr Downer says every country has its renegades and Miss Hanson is one of Australia's.
NEW PLEA FOR APOLOGY FOR FORCED ASSIMILATION POLICIES
The author of the stolen generation report says a formal Federal Government apology is important, because it would acknowledge that past assimilation policies were crimes against humanity.
Human Rights Commissioner, Sir Ronald Wilson, says the policies must be recognised so those affected by them can be healed.
Sir Ronald told a meeting of lawyers, who had gathered to discuss a legal issues paper on the stolen generation, the healing of the heart is important.
He says too many indigenous Australians are scarred from years of not knowing who they are, and from being brought up in a Western society which then rejected them.
PARER WANTS MINING APPROVALS SPED UP
A call by the Federal Resources Minister for mining approvals to be sped up has been greeted with a warning that such moves may put the environment at risk.
Senator Warwick Parer, in the Hunter Region in New South Wales today to open a centre for a joint mining venture, said he would like to see a return to the 1970s, when mines were developed quickly.
Senator Parer says it takes too long for companies to get developments up and running because of duplication by government departments.
But David Noonan, of Minewatch New South Wales, says the Senator's vision is fraught with danger, because all developments should be closely scrutinised.
Mr Noonan says calls for speedy developments usually come from a desire to create jobs quickly, without proper consideration of environmental implications.
WA GOVT MAY BE ABOUT TO GIVE UP SAILING
The Western Australian Government says it would not become involved in another yachting syndicate if the Elle yacht is unable to enter the Whitbread round the world race.
The Court Government has paid half a million dollars to the Elle yachting syndicate as part of a promotional deal with model Elle McPherson.
A further half a million dollars is due at the end of next month provided the yacht enters the race.
The Elle syndicate has not yet paid its race entry fee which was due several weeks ago, but expects to announce a major sponsorship deal on Monday.
Premier Richard Court says he will be disappointed if the Elle yacht is not ready for the start of the race in September.
SINCLAIR SAYS AID TO PNG SHOULD BE LINKED TO CORRUPTION
A senior Federal MP says corruption in Papua New Guinea will influence the aid Australia can give to PNG.
The chairman of Parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, Ian Sinclair, says there should be an indirect link between levels of corruption and aid to Papua New Guinea.
Mr Sinclair says while it is difficult to determine what good governance is, it is not Australia's place to lay down the form of government in a country.
But he says he believes Australia ought to encourage principles whereby those who are in power don't abuse the resonsibilities they have.
Mr Sinclair told the Australian Institute of International Affairs that no country is more important to Australia than Papua New Guinea.
But he said Australia is changing from cash aid to tied projects because some past aid had not been used to help the people.
MOTHS TO HELP RAINFOREST RESEARCH
Scientists say a new discovery, using moths, will lead to better management of rainforests.
In far north Queensland, the Co-operative Research Centre in Cairns has found some groups of moths are found in pristine rainforests while others cluster in disturbed patches.
The Centre's Roger Kitching says the moths can be used to quickly determine the health and biodiversity of rainforests.
Professor Kitching says the discovery will be an important tool in future rainforest research.
FORMER BELLS STAFF STILL OWED WAGES
The union covering staff at former Bells restaurants says the Commonwealth Bank has frozen $630,000 owed in wages.
More than 2,000 workers were made redundant when Bells closed its operations last month.
The Liquor and Hospitality Workers' Union says former staff still have not been paid, and the bank has frozen Bell's liquid assets.
The union's Darren Mathewson says the company is still solvent, but must negotiate a takeover by Wednesday or go into liquidation.
